blocks.content: Every system has slow operations database queries, expensive computations, third-party API calls.
Caching stores the result of a slow operation so the next request for the same data gets it instantly, without re-doing the work.
Compute or fetch something once. Store the result close to where it's needed. Serve it from there for every subsequent request. Speed comes from proximity and skipping repeated work.
1. The core idea
Every layer in a system has a different speed. Caching means promoting data from a slow layer to a fast one.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399124476-91139635.png
A request comes into the system and first checks memory.

["If the data is already in memory, it returns the response immediately.
","If not, it goes to Redis cache which is very fast.
","If Redis has the data, response is returned quickly.
","If Redis misses, it queries the indexed database which is slower.
","If the indexed DB finds the data, it returns the response.
","If not, it falls back to a full database scan which is the slowest.
","Finally, the result is returned as the response.
"]
items: If the data is already in memory, it returns the response immediately.
If not, it goes to Redis cache which is very fast.
If Redis has the data, response is returned quickly.
If Redis misses, it queries the indexed database which is slower.
If the indexed DB finds the data, it returns the response.
If not, it falls back to a full database scan which is the slowest.
Finally, the result is returned as the response.

blocks.content: 2. Cache hit and cache miss
Every cache lookup is either a hit (data found, returned instantly) or a miss (data not found, must fetch from the source). The ratio between them is the hit rate the most important cache metric.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399124478-923792352.png
Request comes with user id and first checks Redis cache.

["If cache hit, response is returned very fast.
","If cache miss, system queries the database.
"]
items: If cache hit, response is returned very fast.
If cache miss, system queries the database.

blocks.content: After getting data from DB, it stores it in cache. Then response is returned. Next time same request comes, it will be served from cache quickly.

["95%+ cache hit means almost all requests are served from cache and DB load is minimal.
","80% hit means cache is helping but still many requests go to DB.
","50% hit means cache is not effective and DB is getting too much traffic.
"]
items: 95%+ cache hit means almost all requests are served from cache and DB load is minimal.
80% hit means cache is helping but still many requests go to DB.
50% hit means cache is not effective and DB is getting too much traffic.

blocks.content: Higher cache hit ratio means better performance and lower latency.
3. TTL : Time To Live
Every cached entry should have an expiry. TTL tells the cache how long to keep data before treating it as stale. Too long and users see outdated data. Too short and the cache barely helps.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785279182492-537808440.png
blocks.alt: A cache entry's TTL lifecycle: written fresh, counts down, then evicted once expired

blocks.content: Every cache entry should expire so stale data is not served.

["Long TTL gives better performance but risks outdated data.
","Short TTL keeps data fresh but reduces cache usefulness.
","Different data needs different TTL based on how often it changes.
","Stable data like product catalog can have very long TTL.
","User data can have medium TTL since it changes sometimes.
","Search results need shorter TTL because they change often.
","Rate limiting needs very short TTL for time windows.
","Live data needs extremely short TTL to stay real-time.
"]
items: Long TTL gives better performance but risks outdated data.
Short TTL keeps data fresh but reduces cache usefulness.
Different data needs different TTL based on how often it changes.
Stable data like product catalog can have very long TTL.
User data can have medium TTL since it changes sometimes.
Search results need shorter TTL because they change often.
Rate limiting needs very short TTL for time windows.
Live data needs extremely short TTL to stay real-time.

blocks.content: 4. Why caching works ( locality )

Caching works because real-world access patterns are not random. A small fraction of data accounts for a huge fraction of requests. This is the 80/20 rule in action 20% of your data gets 80% of the reads.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785279184662-518166850.png
blocks.alt: The 80/20 access pattern: a small hot subset of data serves most of the requests

blocks.content: Most traffic comes from a small portion of data. Around 20% of data is accessed very frequently. This is called hot data and it serves about 80% of requests.
The remaining 80% of data is rarely accessed. This is cold or long-tail data and serves only 20% of requests.
If you cache the hot 20%, you can handle most traffic without hitting the database. This is why caching focuses on frequently accessed data.
What makes a good cache candidate
blocks.text: What makes a good cache candidate

blocks.content:
["Good cache candidates are data that are read many times but updated rarely.
","They are expensive to compute or fetch so caching saves time and resources.
","They can tolerate slight staleness without breaking correctness.
","They are accessed by many users so one cached value serves many requests.
","Bad cache candidates are data that change on every request.
","Data that must always be perfectly accurate should not be cached.
","Highly personalized data with low reuse gives little benefit from caching."]
items: Good cache candidates are data that are read many times but updated rarely.
They are expensive to compute or fetch so caching saves time and resources.
They can tolerate slight staleness without breaking correctness.
They are accessed by many users so one cached value serves many requests.
Bad cache candidates are data that change on every request.
Data that must always be perfectly accurate should not be cached.
Highly personalized data with low reuse gives little benefit from caching.
